According to The Wall Street Journal, Donald Trump reviewed military options for a full-scale war against Iran to “finish the job,” but has decided, for now, not to move forward.

The report says Trump is concerned that renewed military conflict could hurt the chances of a diplomatic resolution and of dismantling Iran’s nuclear program, and that he’s shown willingness to let indirect talks in Qatar run past the August 18 deadline. He is said to be fine with continuing limited strikes on Iranian targets if Tehran violates the current temporary deal - as it already has, repeatedly.

How are those negotiations going?

Not well. It seems JD Vance’s “historic” face-to-face achievement was a one-off. Washington has been quietly downgraded from talking to the Great Satan to negotiating with the Little Satan instead - a senior Qatari official confirmed that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Qatari officials in Doha, but there are currently no high-level U.S.-Iran meetings scheduled.

Faced with Iran publicly denying that peace talks even exist, Vance is denying reality right back, insisting it’s merely a “Persian negotiating tactic.” He’s not wrong that rejectionism is a tactic - he’s just wrong about what it’s negotiating for. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the delegation will skip U.S. officials entirely, meeting only the Qataris in Doha to talk about unfreezing Iran’s own assets. The tactic isn’t stalling for a better peace. It’s stalling for a better payment: extract the MoU concessions first, discuss the nuclear file never.

Iranian officials have shown no willingness to meet U.S. nuclear demands, focusing instead on asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. Reports differ on the nature of the proposed transit fees - Iran calls them mandatory, a regional diplomat calls them voluntary, and Oman’s foreign minister rejects fees outright but leaves room for “maritime service” mechanisms such as safety and pollution measures. Regardless of that distinction, Iran seems set on asserting authority over the waterway: it has already indicated that ships paying “security fees” and following IRGC protocols would get priority transit, while others face delays.

The Met: World-Class Museum, World-Class Fencing Operation

New York’s most respectable art thief just crossed the $95 million line — and still insists it’s the victim, not the fence.

Since 2017, the Manhattan DA has seized more than 120 high-value antiquities from the Met, plus hundreds of “little things” — pottery shards, belt clasps, pins, goddess figurines — with a total value now above $95 million. 

That’s not a rounding error, that’s a business model. We’re talking a 3,700‑year‑old jug from Greece, a marble head, a 2,000‑year‑old bronze Hermes from Turkey, a gold headpiece from ancient Egypt — all politely “repatriated” once investigators show up with subpoenas and old dealer letters.

The Met’s line is pure corporate damage control: we don’t want stolen art, we’re collaborating, we even hired a 12‑person provenance team and put a former Sotheby’s executive in charge. 

We’re building an in‑house crisis unit to manage a scandal we spent decades pretending didn’t exist. The DA’s anti‑trafficking unit is less theatrical: if the museum was really on top of this, they wouldn’t keep finding fresh loot in the galleries every year.

Even the stats fight is revealing. The Met says 198 items seized; prosecutors say 348. The trick? When 20 fragments of a looted Greek cup come in, the Met calls it “one work,” the law calls it 20 separate tagged objects. 

The museum also admits some pieces arrived literally crusted in dirt — a classic red flag for objects yanked straight out of the ground — and kept them anyway. Now those same internal notes are being used as evidence against them.

The biggest tell is how “cooperative” everyone suddenly becomes once the jig is up. 

The Met stresses that in some cases, source countries are graciously leaving tainted pieces in New York on loan, and that relationships with Italy, Greece, Egypt, Turkey and others are “strong.” 

Of course they are: after decades of hoovering up objects through dealers later accused of trafficking, the museum is now negotiating to keep the nicer loot on the wall as a favor.

And sitting like a ghost in the middle of it all is the old network: dealers like Robert Hecht, who sold the Met the Euphronios krater in 1972 for over $1 million, then spent decades being accused of smuggling while museums pretended they had no idea where the goodies came from. 

The krater went back to Italy in 2008. Today, the Met still has dozens of works tied to the same orbit — “under review,” naturally.

So yes, the Met is now very sorry, very transparent, very committed to provenance research. 

But the pattern is clear: the world’s most elite institutions happily built their collections on laundered loot, and only discovered ethics when prosecutors started walking through the front door. 

The gods and heroes in those glass cases weren’t just “donated” — they were collateral in a long, polite crime.
